newsitem.title: FRANCE: French chefs nervously await latest Michelin guide.
newsitem.headline: French chefs nervously await latest Michelin guide.

text.p: France's top chefs were stirring their sauces with trembling hands on Sunday in nervous anticipation of the latest edition of the Michelin guide, the gourmet bible set to reveal its secrets on Monday.

Michelin's publishers were tight-lipped, but rumours and alleged "leaks" were flying in advance of the release of the prestigious volume, which is to France's great chefs what the Oscars are to the Hollywood film industry.
The name on everyone's lips was super-chef Alain Ducasse, who was hoping to become the first chef in Michelin history to run two three-star restaurants simultaneously.

But the betting was that Ducasse would instead win a total of just five stars -- a welcome three for his new Paris restaurant formerly run by the legendary Joel Robuchon, but just two for the glitzy Louis XV in Monaco, whose kitchen he has run since its opening in 1987.
That would mean the loss of a star for the Louis XV, which has held the top three-star rating for the past seven years.
"The rumour is that the Paris restaurant will be given three stars and his restaurant in Monte Carlo, two. We will have no confirmation of that before Monday," said a spokeswoman.
The bright red Michelin, France's most prestigious restaurant guide, bestowed its highest award of three stars to just 19 restaurants last year, down from 20 in 1995.

Michelin rival Gault-Millau, whose bright yellow 1997 guide came out in November, gave its highest rating of four "toques" -- the traditional towering white chef's cap -- to just 12 restaurants this year.

French media reported that chef Michel Bras, whose eponymous restaurant is located in the isolated southwestern town of Laguiole, would be admitted this year into Michelin's exclusive three-star fraternity. His Restaurant Michel Bras now has two stars.
Curiously, Bras closes each year for a "winter" holiday which stretches from November 1 into early April. He could not immediately be reached for comment.
His kitchen specialises in simply prepared dishes using top-quality ingredients and wild herbs. Dinner without wine runs to between 460 and 760 francs ($80-$135) a person.

Another closely watched restaurant on Monday will be the new Paris eatery opened this year by Pierrre Gagnaire, whose three-star restaurant in the depressed central town of Saint Etienne went bankrupt in January 1996.

Several French newspapers have reported matter-of-factly that Gagnaire would win a respectable two stars in the 1997 Michelin though his new place has been open just a few months. He was not immediately available for comment on the reports.

His Saint Etienne restaurant was the first three-star in Michelin history to go bankrupt. He blamed his financial woes on expensive loans, a weak local economy and Parisians' unwillingness to eat at a restaurant in the country without an attached hotel.
Gagnaire's new restaurant in the Hotel Balzac in Paris' Latin Quarter seats just 40. A fixed-price dinner without wine is a relatively reasonable 350 francs ($60).
Ducasse, who is 40, took over the restaurant in Paris' ritzy Parc Victor Hugo Hotel in August from super-chef Robuchon, who retired at 51 after 36 years in the kitchen.
The establishment, which offers classic French cuisine at astronomical prices, changed its name at that time from the Restaurant Joel Robuchon to the Restaurant Alain Ducasse.
Ducasse was just 33 when the Louis XV, which specialises in Mediterranean cuisine and is located in the posh Hotel de Paris near the Monte Carlo casinos, won its third Michelin star.
